defect.snippet:
const updated = await this.repo.update(ticketId, { assigneeId: newAgentId });
    await this.queues.invalidate(updated.assigneeId);

locateQuestion.prompt: Is there a defect in how this code invalidates cached agent queues when tickets change? If so, mark the line(s) where it is; otherwise answer that there is none.
locateQuestion.explanation: reassign() invalidates only updated.assigneeId, which is the new agent. The previous assignee (ticket.assigneeId) still has the ticket in their cached queue for up to 120 seconds, so two agents may work the same ticket. invalidate() already accepts several ids and filters nulls, so it should be called with both ticket.assigneeId and updated.assigneeId.

choiceQuestions.prompt: An unassigned ticket (assigneeId null) has its status set to solved. What does setStatus do to the cache?
choices: It throws because a null key is passed to Redis
It makes no Redis call, because invalidate filters out the null id and skips DEL when no keys remain
It writes an empty queue for the null agent
choiceQuestions.explanation: invalidate() filters nulls, builds an empty key list and returns without calling DEL. There is no wildcard deletion, no SET, and no null key reaches Redis.

choiceQuestions.prompt: Agent X escalates one of their tickets to urgent. When does X's queue reflect the new ordering?
choices: On X's next agentQueue call, which misses the cache and re-sorts from the repo
Never, the cached order is kept until the ticket is solved
Immediately, because escalate rewrites the cached array in place
choiceQuestions.explanation: escalate updates the repo and then deletes agent-queue:X. The next agentQueue call misses, loads from the repo, sorts urgent first, and re-caches. It does not wait for the TTL, and it does not patch the cached array directly.

choiceQuestions.prompt: Why does this design invalidate (delete) the queue rather than update the cached array on each ticket change?
choices: Deleting avoids re-implementing filtering and sorting on each write; the next read rebuilds the queue from the repo
Deleting guarantees no reader can ever observe stale data
Updating in place would require a longer TTL
choiceQuestions.explanation: The queue is a derived view (open tickets for an agent, sorted by priority and age). Deleting and rebuilding on read keeps that logic in one place. The cache stores the array as JSON, so storage is not the issue; deletion narrows but does not eliminate stale windows (a concurrent read can re-fill old data), and TTL is unrelated.
